h: Courting, a hasty wedding and a family that stayed
p: When William Shakespeare married Anne Hathaway in 1582, he was just eighteen and she was twenty-six. Their first child, Susanna, was born six months later, so you can probably guess why the wedding was arranged in a bit of a hurry. Walking round her family home, it's easy to picture a lovestruck young lad trudging over the fields from Stratford to come courting.

Something lovely about this place is how long the Hathaway family stayed. Their descendants lived in the house for generations, and even after the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust bought it in the 1890s, a family member stayed on for some years to show visitors around. That's partly why so much of the family furniture survived.
The thatch hasn't always had an easy time. A fire in 1969 damaged the roof, and it was carefully repaired, which is why it still looks so picture-perfect today.

If the weather's kind, walk there. A footpath runs across the fields from Stratford to Shottery, roughly following the route young Will might have taken, and it's a much more romantic arrival than pulling up in the car. Allow an hour and a half to two hours at the cottage and gardens.

Make it a full Shakespeare day by visiting his birthplace on Henley Street, New Place, where his last family home stood, and Holy Trinity Church, where he's buried. Mary Arden's Farm at Wilmcote, the childhood home of his mother, is a few miles north and great for families. Finish with a stroll along the Avon by the Royal Shakespeare Theatre, or catch a show if you've planned ahead.
